learningObjective: Explain how out-of-SSA translation lowers phi functions into copies at predecessor blocks and identify the swap/lost-copy problem.

canonicalClaims.claim: Phi functions at a merge block have parallel-copy semantics; correct out-of-SSA translation lowers them into copies at predecessor block ends, using temporaries or permutation decomposition to handle cyclic (swap) patterns safely.
conditions: SSA-form IR with phi at merge blocks.
Target ISA lacks a native phi instruction.
nonImplications: Does not imply all phi lowering requires temporaries; only cyclic dependency patterns do.
Does not imply out-of-SSA is the only strategy; SSA-based register allocation is an alternative.

misconceptions.claim: Phi lowering inserts a single move at the merge block.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Phi is a parallel copy fed by predecessor edges; the copies must be placed at each predecessor's end so they execute along the correct incoming edge.

misconceptions.claim: Machine code natively supports phi instructions.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Target ISAs execute a linear stream of instructions; phi is an IR abstraction that must be lowered to explicit copies.

misconceptions.claim: Serializing phi copies in any order is always correct.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Cyclic dependencies (swap patterns) require a temporary or a permutation-preserving schedule; naive sequential copies overwrite needed values.
misconceptions.sourceOrEvidence: Sreedhar et al., Boissinot et al.

implementationFacts: Sreedhar's Method I inserts a temporary per phi in critical cases.
Boissinot's algorithm classifies phi resources by chunks to reduce copy count.
LLVM lowers phi via PHIElimination pass in the machine-IR pipeline.
performanceScenarios: Poor out-of-SSA lowering inserts redundant copies, increasing register pressure and hurting performance.
